newsitem.title: UK: NATO must get act together on weapons - military.
newsitem.headline: NATO must get act together on weapons - military.

text.p: A senior NATO general expressed alarm on Thursday about a growing gap between the defence capabilities of Europe and the United States, and urged European member states to close it.

"The technological advantage the United States enjoys is remarkable. We urgently need to see how we can do better," General Klaus Naumann, head of NATO's Military Committee, told the Royal United Services Institute think-tank.
"We should boost our procurement procedures...We cannot tolerate procurement policies which take so long," he said.

Military experts say the United States is powering ahead with research and development into the next generation of weapons which threaten to turn the mainly European members of NATO into second-class military nations.
"We see the most sophisticated software being used by the United States, which is pouring more money into development," Naumann said.

His comments represented a clear hint that the European NATO members should start considering whether to buy U.S. equipment off the shelf rather than struggling on with costly weapons developments of their own.

Europe's fragmented defence industry already faces a serious challenge from U.S. firms and will be in deeper trouble if plane-makers and defence giants McDonnell Douglas and Boeing Co are allowed to merge as planned.
But Britain and France in particular have influential defence firms and might find it hard to explain politically why they wanted to buy American.
The main European nations cannot even agree on a single main next-generation attack plane, allowing the United States to steal even further ahead.

Britain, Germany, Italy and Spain are supposed to be building the next-generation Eurofighter but the joint project has been delayed by endless arguments over cost. In the meantime, France is concentrating on its own Rafael jet.

NATO also has to find a way of militarily integrating three former Soviet bloc countries -- Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary -- which it is expected to invite in July to open membership negotiations.
The three states have predominantly Soviet-era arms and equipment, which poses another challenge for NATO.

"It will take up to 10 years to fully integrate new members and gain a military interdependency, and this does not take into account military upgrading of new members with western equipment," Naumann said.

"NATO will not ask new members to immediately procure large amounts of western equipment. It will ask that their forces are militarily inter-operable. This is not free but the cost should be modest," he added.

NATO is set to sign a charter next week regulating relations with Russia, which regards the Alliance's expansion plans as a security threat. But Naumann said that even with Moscow reconciled to expansion, more problems remained.

"The process of enlargement will take considerable time and effort. It's possible many doubts will be raised as to the wisdom of NATO enlargement," he said, acknowledging that the expanded bloc could become more unwieldy.
"There is a risk that the sum of all the decisions to be taken could pose a risk for NATO efficiency. We do not neglect these risks," he said.
